judgments.why: X has period detail and asides, such as making amends to the Prussian postal service and his doubts about the route, while Y is a tidy 'My dearest Marie' letter with an invented coffin simile and a signature.
Y is a fragment in a dashed, digressive style with private jokes (the map for the boys, the 'Zierlisel'), while X is a smooth model letter that moralizes about the public.
X is long and vivid, with the trees cut into fans, Kahlenberg and the spelling 'Kaffeh', while Y just restates the card in a generic letter shape.
X has the dry joke about Cousin looking after 'Mrs. Hegel's interests' and the note on cost, while Y wrongly says he arrived in Paris that morning and adds stock family lines.
X has dense lists of church interiors, the Nuremberg aside and the Waterloo sweat joke, while Y is a short polished summary with a signature.
Y is a terse, hurried note with the old spelling 'Cölln', while X pads the card with sentiment about Berlin evenings and card games.
X explains the fish (Besseling is a stricter Catholic than van Ghert) and judges the town hall's architecture, while Y is formulaic and adds advice on the boys' studies.
X is a long rambling account with the woollen linings against the cold, frustration with the post coaches, the Peter joke and a harsh verdict on the cathedral, while Y is a bland summary.
Y compares the cafés to the Berlin 'tents' and remarks on philistines and Berliner-looking faces, while X is generic and moralizing ('pure sensuous life').
Y is a dated postscript with a wordplay ('so far, or rather so near'), while X invents a conversation and a critique of Schlegel.
Y has rich idiosyncratic detail (Wolff's 'sloth' pun, the actor Blum, the Göttingen jab, chicory coffee), while X invents a moral lesson about the Englishman.
Y has the tender reply to Immanuel ('no longer such a small springing-about fellow'), while X brings in an anachronistic boast about Napoleon's camp at Jena and a curt tone.
Y is a brief, plausible aside on the small theatres, while X gets Pesaroni's sex wrong ('his reputation'), though she was a contralto.
X has concrete logistics (up at 3, the hills, on foot until 11½) and a description of the Moselle valley, while Y moralizes about freedom and the old world order.
X is a hurried farewell written at the table in the shorthand 'Mr. v. Gh.', while Y is a padded letter with stock snuff and rest lines.
Y is a clipped note comparing the flowers to the Peacock Island, while X turns the passage into a heavy-handed allegory of state power.
X gives a full route, Egmont in Kassel, the Griesheim family and the deaf Grand Duke, while Y is a short generic letter that ends wrongly at 'nearly ten'.
Y is a single natural sentence with the detail of the Koblenz road branching off, while X invents a lecture on disciplining the boys.
Y is a spontaneous, relieved note, while X garbles the logistics and adds a 'freedom is the end of all striving' cliché.
Y is an elliptical fragment with the wish that the young ones were there and the line that you would not be too old for it, while X is philosophizing filler.
X is excited and elliptical, with the garbled time on the playbill and the 'antique heads', while Y calls the singing merely competent and adds stock lines about the boys.
Y starts mid-sentence and carries detail such as the eye-water spring and the Culm battlefield, while X is a smooth summary with an invented quarrel about wine.
X is a long, idiosyncratic account (25 francs to Paris, the three-master as a Sultan, Mrs. Voß's gardens, tying his neckerchief), while Y is a generic reflection on the North Sea.
Y has a wry joke ('I myself have only known it for half an hour'), while X pads the one-line card with domestic sentiment.
